table: Passing of traits from parents to offspring
Differences among individuals of a species; very little in asexual reproduction, more in sexual reproduction
A section of DNA that carries the information for a protein, and so for a trait
Expressed even if only one copy is present (T)
Expressed only when both copies are recessive (tt)
Gene make-up (TT, Tt, tt) / visible trait (tall, short)

bullets: Why pea: many clear contrasting traits, short life cycle, self-pollinating but easy to cross, many seeds.
**Monohybrid cross:** TT (tall) × tt (short) → F_{1} all tall (Tt). F_{1} × F_{1} → F_{2}: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
F_{2} ratios: **phenotype 3 tall : 1 short**; **genotype 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt**.
The short trait is not lost in F_{1}. It is hidden by the dominant trait and reappears in F_{2}.
**Dihybrid cross:** RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green) → F_{1} all RrYy (round yellow).
F_{2}: **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**, so traits are inherited **independently**.

box: **Checkerboard for Tt × Tt.** Gametes from each parent: T and t.
T × T = TT (tall) · T × t = Tt (tall) · t × T = Tt (tall) · t × t = tt (short)

blocks.p: Gene → protein (often an enzyme) → trait. Example: an efficient enzyme makes more growth hormone, so the plant is tall. An altered gene gives a less efficient enzyme, less hormone, and a short plant. Each parent gives **one copy** of each gene to the offspring through the germ cells.

bullets: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. One pair is the sex chromosomes.
Mother: XX, so every egg carries X. Father: XY, so half the sperm carry X and half carry Y.
X sperm + egg → XX (girl). Y sperm + egg → XY (boy). So the **father's sperm decides** the sex. The chance is 50 : 50.
In some animals the environment decides sex: in some reptiles, the temperature at which eggs are kept. Some snails can change sex.
Writing the F_{2} ratio as 1 : 2 : 1 when the question asks for the **phenotypic** ratio (3 : 1).
Saying the mother decides the sex of the child.
Forgetting to show gametes in a cross. They carry marks!
